title: Pharmaceutics III — Lecture 1: Preformulation
summary: Preformulation is the physicochemical investigation of a drug substance alone and/or when combined with excipients before formulation.
It bridges drug discovery and pharmaceutical manufacturing and ensures a stable, effective, and manufacturable final product.
Goals of preformulation include establishing physicochemical parameters, aiding dosage form design, and studying drug-excipient compatibility.
Studies included in preformulation are organoleptic properties, purity, particle size, polymorphism, solubility, and dissolution.
Physical description includes color, odor, and taste; color relates to unsaturation and chromophores, while odor and taste relate to major functional groups.
Purity estimates known and significant impurities and can be assessed by TLC, HPLC, GC, and DSC.
Microscopic examination provides particle size, size range, crystal structure, particle shape, crystal habit, surface characteristics, agglomeration, and polymorphic differences.
Melting point depression can indicate drug-excipient compatibility and eutectic mixture formation.
A eutectic mixture melts at a temperature lower than either pure component alone; salol-thymol eutectic melts at 13°C at 65% salol.
Tablets are the most common oral solid dosage form and require the drug to be in a solid, compressible form.
Liquid APIs can be formulated as oral solutions/suspensions, soft gelatin capsules, solid ester or salt forms, or solid carriers such as melted PEG in hard gelatin capsules.
Particle size governs physical stability, solubility, dissolution rate, flow, sedimentation, and bioavailability.
Micronization increases dissolution rate for poorly water-soluble drugs such as griseofulvin and spironolactone, while macrocrystalline nitrofurantoin slows dissolution to reduce GI upset.
Polymorphism is the ability of an API to exist in multiple crystal lattice structures with identical molecular formula; amorphous forms are more soluble, crystalline forms are more stable.
Solubility is required for oral drugs to dissolve in GIT fluids before absorption; insoluble compounds show incomplete or erratic absorption.
Strategies to overcome poor solubility include chemical modification, salt formation, co-solvents, surfactants, solid dispersions, micronization, and novel delivery platforms.
The equilibrium solubility method determines solubility by adding excess drug to solvent, shaking at constant temperature until equilibrium, and analyzing the solution.
Ostwald-Freundlich equation relates solubility and particle size: log(S/S0) = 2γV / (2.303RT r).
Solubility of ionizable drugs depends on pH and pKa; for weak acids, S = Sa[1 + Ka/H+].
A weak acid drug can precipitate when pH drops because it converts from soluble ionized form to insoluble un-ionized free acid form.

keyTerms.definition: The physicochemical investigation of a drug substance alone and/or when combined with excipients to establish fundamental physical and chemical properties before formulation.
A mixture of two solid substances that, when mixed in a particular ratio, melts at a temperature lower than the melting point of either substance alone.
The ability of an active pharmaceutical ingredient to exist in multiple crystal lattice structures while retaining identical molecular formula.
A solid form that is more soluble than the crystalline form.
A solid form that is more stable than the amorphous form.
The amount of drug absorbed is not consistent from one dose to another or from one patient to another.
A method where excess drug is placed in solvent, shaken at constant temperature until equilibrium, and the solution is analyzed to determine dissolved drug.
An equation relating solubility and particle size: log(S/S0) = 2γV / (2.303RT r).
Equation calculating total solubility of a weakly acidic drug as a function of hydrogen ion concentration.
Particle size reduction that increases specific surface area and dissolution rate for poorly water-soluble drugs.
